claims.text: Adding a trace amount of chromium to a boride-based component will promote in situ formation of a chromium-rich oxide scale during hot-dip aluminum plating.
The chromium-rich oxide scale will reduce molten-aluminum corrosion.
Chromium may be introduced into the component by surface alloying or diffusion treatment.
Typical hot-dip aluminum-plating exposure occurs at approximately 660°C.
A local chromium concentration of roughly 1–3 wt.% is an optimal range for the treatment.
A local chromium concentration of roughly 1–3 wt.% can be introduced without altering the component's bulk properties.
The treatment will produce a dense, continuous chromium-rich oxide layer at the surface or interface of the boride component.
Chromium in the treated layer will preferentially oxidize during exposure to high-temperature molten aluminum.
The resulting chromium oxide will be stable under molten-aluminum exposure and act as a diffusion barrier.
The chromium-rich oxide barrier will limit molten-aluminum penetration and direct interaction with the boride matrix.
Chromium-treated boride components will have a lower corrosion rate than untreated boride components.
Chromium-treated boride components will retain better surface integrity than untreated components.
Chromium treatment will reduce elemental interdiffusion at the component–molten-aluminum interface.
Untreated boride-based components typically develop unprotected surfaces that permit relatively rapid molten-aluminum attack and corrosion.
The protective effect should remain effective under standard hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions.
Chromium levels below the amount required for a continuous oxide will not provide the proposed protection.
Excessive chromium may alter other material properties and negate the intervention's effectiveness.
The intervention may be ineffective when process parameters do not facilitate formation of the oxide scale.
